memoryText: This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Luke 22:19 slowly, several times, and say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Jesus says this at the table on the night before his death. He takes the Passover bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and gives it to his disciples. In a few hours he will be arrested, and he knows it.

“This is my body.” At the Passover, Israel ate bread and remembered the exodus. Jesus takes the bread of that meal and attaches it to himself. His body will be broken, and the true exodus from sin and death will come through him. Christians have understood the exact nature of the bread in different ways, but all hold that this meal is about Christ.

“Which is given for you.” The word “for” is the heart of the gospel. He is not simply a martyr or an example. His body is given in your place, on your behalf. And it is personal: for you.

“Do this.” Jesus gives a command. The Lord’s Supper is not optional for the church. It is a gift and an instruction, and it has been kept for two thousand years.

“In remembrance of me.” To remember in the Bible is more than recalling a fact. It is to bring the past into the present, to be fed by it, and to proclaim it. When we take the bread and the cup, we look back to the cross, look up to the risen Christ, and look forward to the day he comes again.

When you doubt that you are loved, say this verse. His body was given for you.
weekInReview: This week you read Psalm 31:19-24, where the goodness of God is stored up for those who fear him, and Psalm 41 and Psalm 55, where David’s own friend lifted his heel against him, and where he learned to cast his burden on the LORD. In Luke 19 to 21 the King rode into Jerusalem, wept over it, cleansed the temple, and silenced every question. He praised a poor widow and spoke of his return. In Luke 22 and 23 you came to the upper room, where Jesus gave the bread and the cup of the new covenant, and to Gethsemane, where he prayed, “Not my will, but yours.” You watched him be betrayed with a kiss, denied by Peter, mocked, declared innocent three times, and handed over to the crowd in place of Barabbas.
reflectionQuestions: Jesus said his body was given “for you” and his blood poured out for you. What does it mean to you personally that he did this?
In Gethsemane, Jesus prayed, “Not my will, but yours, be done.” How does his submission to the Father shape the way you pray when you face something hard?
Peter denied Jesus, and Jesus looked at him. Where do you need to receive that look of love, rather than of condemnation?
prayerPrompts: Remember Jesus with the bread and the cup, in your own words.
Thank him for his body given and his blood poured out.
